purpose: A code base is read by a maintainer, a person or an AI, who comes to change it at any time after it is written. Reading each part once, they understand it, find the one place a change belongs, and make the change without breaking another behavior, in a short time.

checklist.what: When the maintainer reads a name, such as of a variable, a function, a module or a constant, can they say what it holds or does without reading where it is defined?
checklist.why: If yes, the maintainer reads each line on its own and gets it right. A value that means something, such as a limit, has a name that says what it means. If no, the maintainer goes to each definition and back, or guesses; a wrong guess about what a name holds becomes a fault in the line they write next.
grounds: Google, "What to look for in a code review" (google/eng-practices), Naming: "A good name is long enough to fully communicate what the item is or does".
Google Python Style Guide, Naming: "Names should be descriptive." and "Avoid abbreviation."

examples.fails:
def proc(d, rs):
    return [r for r in rs if r.cap >= d.n and d.eq <= r.eq]
examples.passes:
def rooms_that_fit(meeting, rooms):
    return [room for room in rooms if room.seats >= meeting.attendees and meeting.equipment <= room.equipment]

checklist.what: Each time the maintainer meets a name, can they tell rightly whether it names a thing they have already met, and which one?
checklist.why: If yes, the maintainer keeps one picture of each thing across the whole code base, and the code's names are the words the product's users use for the same things. If no, a maintainer who meets a second name for one thing takes it for a second thing and writes code for both, and one who meets one name for two things changes both when they meant one.
grounds: Fowler, "UbiquitousLanguage" (martinfowler.com): "building up a common, rigorous language between developers and users", which "should be based on the Domain Model used in the software."

examples.fails: room in the matcher, space in the API and venue in the calendar link, all for one Room; booking for a request in one module and for a confirmed hold in another.
examples.passes: room everywhere; BookingRequest for what the worker asks, and Booking for what is held.

checklist.what: After reading any function once from the top, can the maintainer say in one sentence what it does?
checklist.why: If yes, the maintainer understands each function in one reading and changes it without breaking a part they did not see. A function does one thing, at one level: a long one reads as calls to functions named for their steps. If no, the maintainer holds many steps and branches in mind at once, misses one, and the change they make breaks it.
grounds: Google, "What to look for in a code review" (google/eng-practices), Complexity: "“Too complex” usually means “can't be understood quickly by code readers.”" and "It can also mean “developers are likely to introduce bugs when they try to call or modify this code.”"

examples.fails: book(request), eighty lines nested four deep, reads the request, matches the rooms, writes the hold and emails the worker.
examples.passes: book(request) reads as four calls: read_request, rooms_that_fit, hold and send_confirmation, each a function of its own.

checklist.what: When the maintainer meets code that looks wrong or roundabout, can they tell from a comment beside it why it is so, before they change it?
checklist.why: If yes, the maintainer keeps what the code needs and simplifies only what it does not, because each reason the code cannot show, such as a limit outside it or a way not taken, is said where it applies. If no, the maintainer tidies away a line that was there for a reason, and the fault it guarded against comes back.
grounds: Google, "What to look for in a code review" (google/eng-practices), Comments: "Usually comments are useful when they explain why some code exists, and should not be explaining what some code is doing."

examples.fails: time.sleep(1) between two calendar writes, alone. (The maintainer removes it, and the calendar refuses bookings at the morning peak.)
examples.passes:
# The calendar refuses more than one write per second for a calendar; wait so a burst of bookings is not refused.
time.sleep(1)

checklist.what: When the maintainer moves from one module to another, do they find the same kind of thing done the same way, such as an error reported, an input checked or a file laid out?
checklist.why: If yes, what the maintainer learns in one module holds in the next, and a difference they meet means a real difference. The code follows its language's style guide and the ways the code base already has. If no, the maintainer learns each module's way anew, takes a difference of habit for one of meaning, and the code they add makes a third way.
grounds: Google, "What to look for in a code review" (google/eng-practices), Consistency: "If no other rule applies, the author should maintain consistency with the existing code."
Google Python Style Guide, "Parting Words": "If code you add to a file looks drastically different from the existing code around it, it throws readers out of their rhythm when they go to read it."

examples.fails: One handler of the Booking API raises ValueError on a bad input, another returns None, and a third returns {"error": ...}.
examples.passes: Every handler raises BadRequest with what was wrong, and one place turns it into the response.

checklist.what: When the maintainer changes one rule or one piece of knowledge, such as how a fit is judged or how long a hold lasts, do they change it in one place only?
checklist.why: If yes, the change is made once and holds everywhere, because each rule is written once and the rest uses it. If no, the maintainer changes the places they find and leaves the rest, and the code then gives two answers to one question, often in a case no test reaches.
grounds: Hunt and Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer (1999), DRY: "Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system."

examples.fails: The 15-minute hold is written as 15 in api/hold.py, as 900 seconds in calendar/link.py, and again in the release job.
examples.passes: HOLD = timedelta(minutes=15) stands in api/hold.py, and every other place imports it.

checklist.what: Whichever line the maintainer reads, code or comment, would they lose something they need if it were removed?
checklist.why: If yes, the maintainer's reading goes to what the code does and why. Code that never runs, code left commented out, an unused import or parameter, and a comment that says again what the line below it says give the maintainer nothing; unlike a behavior no case needs, they give no behavior at all. If no, each such line is read, kept and changed with the rest, and a comment that restates the code is left behind when the code changes and then tells the maintainer the wrong thing.
grounds: Google, "What to look for in a code review" (google/eng-practices), Comments: "Usually comments are useful when they explain why some code exists, and should not be explaining what some code is doing." and "If the code isn't clear enough to explain itself, then the code should be made simpler."

examples.fails:
# loop over the rooms
for room in rooms:
    ...
# old_matcher(meeting)  (commented out, with an import used nowhere above it)
examples.passes:
for room in rooms:
    ...  (the old matcher is in the version history, not in the file)

checklist.what: When the maintainer runs the tests from before the code was bettered against the code after it, each test's expected result left as it was, does every test pass?
checklist.why: If yes, bettering the code changed only how it says what it does, so whoever relies on the code gets the same behavior. The tests call the code as its callers do, so they stand while its insides change; a call is changed only where a name it uses was renamed. If no, a behavior changed under the name of tidying, and the change is hidden among many that change nothing; a test that fails though no behavior changed was written against the code's insides, and fails again on the next betterment.
grounds: Fowler, refactoring.com: "Refactoring is a disciplined technique for restructuring an existing body of code, altering its internal structure without changing its external behavior."
Winters, Manshreck and Wright, Software Engineering at Google, ch. 12 "Unit Testing": "Only breaking changes in a system's behavior should require going back to change its tests".

examples.fails: Tidying rooms_that_fit makes it return a set, and its tests are changed to expect a set. (The offered rooms lose their order.)
examples.passes: rooms_that_fit is split into seats_fit and equipment_fits inside; the tests from before pass unchanged.
